source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 87-91 = PDF pp. 1-5, all pages read on renders at 150 dpi; Figures 1 and 2 (p. 89) extracted at their native 1000 ppi and read by pixel measurement against the axis ticks (Figure 2 bar tops within 0.1 of whole numbers; Figure 1 markers within 0.02 of sixths). Step 1 written before the card was opened.

claims.overstatement: No material overstatement; the claim states the fixed order, the missing no-voucher condition, the laboratory setting and the untested treatment extension. Minor wording points. (1) 'with small, immediate rewards': the voucher was handed over at once, but it could be exchanged for $5 in money, or for a $5 store voucher, only at discharge (p. 88, Procedure, 2nd paragraph; p. 89, top of left column), so the non-drug reward was delayed while the cocaine was immediate; suggest 'small rewards (cash or goods only at discharge)'. (2) 'at 50 mg about 4 times in 5 (3.8 and 4.5 of 5)': 77% and 90%; the merchandise figure is nearer 9 in 10. (3) 'cannot be separated from the order of the sessions' is right by design; the authors acknowledged this and argued, from their other studies and participants' reports, that order effects were unlikely (p. 90), which the claim could mention.
claims.note: Re-found and re-measured blind: participants (4 women, 2 men, 30-39 years, mean 36; New York City, word of mouth and newspaper advertisements; almost daily smoked cocaine; $100-$500 a week, mean $280; treatment seeking not stated) p. 88; fixed order money then merchandise, one dose per session, sample + 5 choices at 14-min intervals, FR 200 p. 88; F(3, 15) = 15.26 and F(1, 5) = 7.48 p. 89. My pixel readings of Figure 2 (15/16, 7/7, 12/14, 12/16, 2/7, 16/17; means 10.67 and 12.83) and Figure 1 (money 0.67, 2.50, 3.67, 3.83; merchandise 1.50, 2.67, 4.17, 4.50) equal the claim's. Editors' calculations recomputed and reproduced: paired difference 2.167 (SD 1.941, SE 0.792), t = 2.735, t squared = 7.478 = printed F; 95% CI 0.130 to 4.203; dz 1.116; active doses 60 and 68 of 90 (66.7% and 75.6%); 0-mg share 0.833 of 2.167 = 38.5%; per-dose 2.5/2.67 at 12 mg. Overall, including dummy-dose sessions, cocaine was chosen on 64 and 77 of 120 trials (53% and 64%), so 'most occasions' is a bare majority with the money voucher.

anchors.extracted: Six experienced cocaine smokers (two men, four women), inpatient; a $5 money or merchandise voucher as the alternative; each session one sample trial then five choice trials; eight sessions pairing each dose (0, 12, 25, 50 mg) with each voucher type; choices rose with dose and were fewer with money vouchers; the authors generalize to people who use cocaine.

Earlier laboratory work cited, not read here: Higgins et al. (1994a), intranasal cocaine choice fell as the money alternative's value rose; animal studies with non-drug alternatives; the laboratory had used merchandise vouchers to reduce the chance of buying cocaine after the study; the design is called double-blind.

4 women (3 African-American, 1 Hispanic) and 2 men (Caucasian), aged 30-39 (mean 36), recruited by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements in New York City; all reported almost daily smoked cocaine use and spending $100-$500 (mean $280) a week; screened medically and psychologically; no statement on treatment seeking.
Participants lived at a hospital clinical research centre for the whole study, could leave only with staff, no visitors; tobacco allowed outside sessions.

Eight sessions each: sessions 1-4 offered a voucher exchangeable for $5 in money at discharge, sessions 5-8 one exchangeable for a $5 store voucher at discharge (money always first); one cocaine dose level per session (0, 12, 25 or 50 mg); a sample trial then five choice trials 14 minutes apart; each option required 200 spacebar presses; doses given only within heart-rate and blood-pressure limits.

Eyes closed during dosing to hide dose cues; one inhalation of cocaine base per chosen dose; a voucher for cash or merchandise when the non-drug option was chosen, all vouchers redeemable only at the end of the study.

Cocaine choice increased with dose, F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001, and was lower with the money voucher, F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05; no significant interaction; no significant voucher difference at any single dose; all but one participant chose more cocaine with the merchandise voucher.

Mean cocaine choices of 5 (error bars SEM), money vs merchandise, read by pixel measurement: 0 mg 0.67 vs 1.50; 12 mg 2.50 vs 2.67; 25 mg 3.67 vs 4.17; 50 mg 3.83 vs 4.50 (all sixths; sums 64 and 77 as in Figure 2). Active doses 60 vs 68 of 90 choices; the dummy dose supplies 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%).

Total cocaine choices of 20 per person, money vs merchandise, read by pixel measurement: 15/16, 7/7, 12/14, 12/16, 2/7, 16/17; means 10.67 vs 12.83 (asterisk on the mean comparison only). Editors' calculation: paired difference 2.17, 95% CI 0.13 to 4.20, dz 1.12; t squared 7.48 equals the printed F. Unlabelled error bars on the means reach 16.0 and 17.5, i.e. +1 SD of the six totals, not SEM.
Earlier studies (Higgins et al. 1994a intranasal; Hatsukami et al. 1994 smoked) found cocaine intake fell as the money alternative's value rose; these were not read for this claim.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in right column)
anchors.extracted: About two fewer of 20 doses with money ('10% more effective'); no condition without a voucher, so the absolute influence of either voucher cannot be quantified; order not randomized (cash first), so cocaine's effects may have changed over the study; the authors judge this unlikely (stable patterns in their other studies; all participants reported using substantially more cocaine outside the laboratory than in sessions).
Authors extend the finding to outpatient contingency management (cash or larger vouchers would further enhance abstinence) and cite Chutuape et al. 1999; abstinence was not measured in this study.

key_findings.correction: Figure 2 readings and editors' calculation reproduced independently by pixel measurement and recomputation.
Figure 1 readings reproduced independently (markers within 0.02 of the stated sixths).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: cap heights 16.0 and 17.5 = mean + SD (15.95, 17.46); mean + SEM would be 12.8 and 14.7.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high is right: the voucher comparison is completely confounded with period. Note for the editor: METHODS 5.3 reserves RoB 2 for laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order, which this voucher comparison lacks (ROBINS-I would be the protocol's match for a non-randomized comparison of interventions); the overall judgment would be the most severe level either way.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: abstract generalization, untested $5.50 proportionality, and the abstinence extension.

missed: The vouchers were exchangeable for money or goods only at discharge (p. 88, Procedure, 2nd paragraph; p. 89, top), so the alternative was a delayed reward set against an immediate dose; the merchandise voucher was itself a voucher for a store voucher. This bears on how strong an alternative was tested and on the claim's phrase 'immediate rewards'.
